claims.text: Alloying the Cr coating with approximately 5–10 at.% Al by co-sputtering will produce an Al-doped Cr coating capable of forming an interfacial oxide barrier.
During high-temperature steam exposure, Al in the Cr matrix will oxidize preferentially.
Preferential Al oxidation will form a nanometer-scale, continuous Al2O3 interlayer specifically at the buried Cr/Zr interface.
The interfacial Al2O3 layer will be dense and adherent.
The interfacial Al2O3 layer will be self-healing.
The Al2O3 barrier will limit atomic diffusion between the Cr-based coating and the Zr-alloy substrate.
Limiting Cr–Zr interdiffusion will mitigate formation of detrimental interdiffusion-induced phases.
At approximately 1000–1200 °C in steam, the Al2O3 barrier will form rapidly enough to protect the interface during 1–5 hour transients.
Under high-temperature steam, Al-doped Cr will exhibit significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion than an elemental Cr coating.
At approximately 320 °C in 11–12 MPa subcritical water, Al oxidation will be sufficiently slow to prevent significant Al2O3 formation for exposures up to 60 days.
The Al-doped Cr coating will maintain corrosion protection comparable to elemental Cr during subcritical-water exposure.
An elemental Cr coating provides adequate baseline corrosion protection under subcritical-water conditions.
An elemental Cr coating undergoes accelerated Cr–Zr interdiffusion during high-temperature steam exposure.
High-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion causes premature degradation of the elemental Cr coating.
The proposed benefit is primarily confined to operation near 320 °C and transient steam exposure at approximately 1000–1200 °C.
Temperatures or exposure durations outside the specified boundaries may alter the kinetics of formation of the proposed interfacial oxide.
